answer: When threads within the same warp take different execution paths (i.e., branch divergence), this causes performance problems and is generally discouraged. According to CUDA optimization guidance, it is a high-priority recommendation to avoid different execution paths within the same warp, since flow control instructions can cause threads to diverge and execute different code paths, which reduces efficiency. Additionally, Independent Thread Scheduling—a feature that allows threads to progress independently through divergent code paths—can lead to a different set of threads participating in operations (such as collective or warp-synchronous operations) than would be expected under the traditional lockstep execution model, potentially causing subtle correctness issues if code assumes all threads in a warp are executing in unison.

answer: Shared memory bank conflicts arise when multiple threads in a warp access different addresses that map to the same memory bank—for example, this can happen when copying a tile from global memory into shared memory in a way that causes multiple threads to hit the same bank simultaneously. To minimize these conflicts, it is important to understand how memory addresses map to memory banks and to schedule memory requests optimally so that threads access different banks in parallel rather than colliding on the same one. Additionally, adjusting the shared memory bank size (a configuration option available on some architectures) is a technique that can be used to help avoid conflicts, and importantly, changing this bank size does not increase shared memory usage or negatively affect occupancy, making it a low-cost way to address bank conflicts.

answer: Memory coalescing is a very important performance consideration when programming CUDA-capable GPU architectures, and it applies specifically to accesses to global memory ("Coalesced Access to Global Memory"). The core rule is that memory transactions should be aligned and grouped so that threads' individual small accesses combine into larger efficient transactions rather than being handled inefficiently one at a time. For example, if each thread only accesses 4 bytes but a 32-byte memory transaction is generated per thread's 4-byte access, this indicates inefficient (non-coalesced) memory access, since much of the transferred data goes unused relative to what is actually requested. This guidance is documented as part of the CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide (Release 13.3), which provides recommendations for achieving high performance on GPU hardware, including proper coalescing of global memory accesses.
